lesson.title: Turning Off Escaping: Raw Strings
lesson.summary: Prefixing a string literal with r turns off escape-sequence processing, treating backslashes as literal characters, which is essential for file paths and regular expressions.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter on Escape Characters ended with a real problem: a string like "C:\new\folder" looks like a Windows file path, but Python reads \n inside it as a newline escape character, silently mangling the path into something with a line break in the middle of it instead of the two backslash characters you intended. Raw strings exist to solve exactly this kind of situation, by telling Python to turn off escape-sequence processing for an entire string literal.

You create a raw string by placing the letter r immediately before the opening quotation mark, with no space between them: r"C:\new\folder". Inside a raw string, a backslash is treated as a literal backslash character, full stop, no matter what letter follows it. Trace through print(r"C:\new\folder") versus print("C:\new\folder"): the raw version prints exactly what it looks like, C:\new\folder, with the backslashes intact as backslashes, while the non-raw version prints "C:", then a line break, then "ew\folder", because \n was interpreted as an escape sequence, silently corrupting the path.

Raw strings are especially important once you start working with regular expressions, a text-pattern-matching tool built into Python's re module, because regular expression syntax uses the backslash constantly for its own purposes, completely separate from Python's escape sequences. A pattern meant to match a literal period, for instance, is written \. in regular expression syntax. If you write that as a normal string, "\.", Python does not recognize \. as one of its own escape sequences, so it happens to leave it alone in this particular case, but many other regex patterns, like \d for a digit or \s for whitespace, can collide with characters that mean something different, or trigger a warning, under Python's own escaping rules, producing confusing or subtly wrong behavior. Writing r"\." and r"\d" sidesteps the whole issue by guaranteeing the backslash reaches the regex engine unchanged.

There is one sharp edge worth knowing: a raw string still cannot end in a single unescaped backslash, because Python's parser needs to know where the string ends, and a trailing backslash would appear to be escaping the closing quote itself. Writing r"C:\path\" is a SyntaxError for this reason, even though it looks like it should mean "end the string right after that backslash." If you truly need a trailing backslash in a raw string, the usual workaround is to add it outside the raw string with concatenation, like r"C:\path" + "\\".

Raw strings do not create a different type of string, they only change how the literal is parsed at the moment Python reads your source code. Once the string exists as a value in memory, r"C:\new\folder" and a correctly escaped "C:\\new\\folder" are indistinguishable, equal in every way, including under == comparison. Raw strings are purely a convenience for writing the literal itself, most valuable anywhere backslashes are common: file paths, and especially regular expressions.
